title: Time's Up for the Gang

jokes.text: Charlie rushing to get a 'good seat' at a sexual harassment seminar
jokes.setup: Charlie announces he wants to get a good seat, implying excitement for something fun
jokes.punchline: It's a sexual harassment seminar — there are no 'good seats,' and Charlie's enthusiasm is completely misplaced
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie Kelly obliviousness. His eager front-row energy for a seminar he has no comprehension of is perfectly in character. The mismatch between his enthusiasm and the gravity of the topic is the entire joke, and it lands because Charlie's child-like confusion is a core character trait.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'There are no good seats. Where are you going?' Charlie: 'Up front.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the obvious absurdity of wanting a good seat at a harassment seminar
jokes.punchline: Charlie has already committed to going up front, completely ignoring the correction
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure of Dennis's exasperated correction immediately undercut by Charlie simply saying 'Up front' is tight and efficient. It doubles down on Charlie's obliviousness without overstaying the welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 'Back in the day, I banged all my secretaries. That's the way you did it. You hire some girl with no experience, you bang her, you promote her. It's a win-win situation for everybody, except for the wives.'

jokes.text: Mac: 'This is so unfair. I mean, I'm not saying it doesn't happen to loads of women all the time, but I don't harass anybody, so why am I here?'
jokes.setup: Mac is about to object to being at the seminar on grounds of his own innocence
jokes.punchline: He prefaces it with a grudging acknowledgment that harassment is real and widespread, then pivots immediately to self-exemption — the classic bad-faith 'I'm not saying BUT' construction
jokes.explanation: The joke skewers a very specific rhetorical bad-faith move — the 'I acknowledge the problem exists, but it doesn't apply to me' dodge — and Mac is the perfect vessel for it. It's observational comedy through character. Well-constructed and topically sharp.

dialogue.line: You DENNIS'd someone probably

jokes.text: Frank: 'Back in the day, I banged all my secretaries. You hire some girl with no experience, you bang her, you promote her. It's a win-win situation for everybody, except for the wives.'
jokes.setup: The group is at a sexual harassment seminar to reform their behavior
jokes.punchline: Frank cheerfully describes systematic workplace sexual exploitation as a sensible, mutually beneficial business arrangement, with the wives as the only real losers
jokes.explanation: This is Frank at his best. The 'win-win except for the wives' capper is pitch-perfect — it's not just that he did it, it's that he's genuinely analyzed the stakeholders and reached a logical conclusion that excludes the most obvious victim (the secretary) while identifying a different one (wives). The cheerful self-incrimination in a room specifically designed to address this behavior is deliciously on-brand. Earns a high craft score for structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The only reason we're here is because you DENNIS'd someone probably and she put us on the list.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Frank, modulate your volume.' / 'The future of Paddy's depends on us completing this seminar.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to be the responsible one who gets everyone through the seminar
jokes.punchline: His entire concern is reputational/financial, not ethical — he explicitly doesn't care about the content, only completing the requirement
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Dennis playing the 'responsible adult' while being entirely amoral. It's not a sharp joke on its own but sets up the irony of his later reveal. Mid-tier setup work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Who could possibly be happy right now?

dialogue.speaker: Instructor
dialogue.line: Hey-o! Who's ready to party?!

jokes.text: 'The only reason we're here is because you DENNIS'd someone probably and she put us on the list.'
jokes.setup: The gang is blaming each other for being on the list
jokes.punchline: 'DENNIS'd' has become a verb — the implication that Dennis's predatory behavior is so systematic and well-known that it has its own verb form
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Using 'DENNIS'd' as a verb is elegant, economical, and loaded — it rewards show-watchers who know Dennis's 'D.E.N.N.I.S. System' (a previous episode's running joke) while still landing for newcomers as a character indictment. The casualness of 'probably' elevates it further. High craft, highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: How many points do we need to score?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Everything is graded by points because how could the Eagles have won the Super Bowl?

jokes.text: Dee: 'Yeah, you perv. You happy now? You happy?'
jokes.setup: Mac has just laid out that Dennis is probably responsible for the list
jokes.punchline: Dee piles on with gleeful aggression, her eagerness to attack Dennis being funnier than any specific accusation
jokes.explanation: Adequate pile-on beat. Dee's opportunistic attack on Dennis is consistent with her character but the line itself isn't particularly clever. Functions as a crowd-pleaser reaction to Mac's sharper joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Everything is graded by points, right? I mean, otherwise, how could the Eagles have won the Super Bowl, right?

jokes.text: Dennis's anxious monologue: 'Women are on a little bit of a rampage right now and anyone could be taken down at any moment... Who could possibly be happy right now?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to deflect blame from himself while expressing genuine existential panic about the #MeToo moment
jokes.punchline: His paranoid, self-centered framing — treating a cultural reckoning as a personal threat to his lifestyle — culminates in 'Who could possibly be happy right now?' setting up the immediate undercut
jokes.explanation: The setup for the immediate visual gag that follows. Dennis's escalating spiral reads as genuinely unhinged self-interest disguised as social awareness. Works best as the straight-man setup to the cold open gag that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: They got nothing on me past '92, tops

jokes.text: Immediately after Dennis's 'Who could possibly be happy right now?' — the seminar host bursts in singing 'Time's up, time's up!' with party energy
jokes.setup: Dennis asks 'Who could possibly be happy right now?' with genuine dread
jokes.punchline: Cut to: an enthusiastic woman singing a cheerful 'Time's Up' anthem as if arriving at a party — the irony that the seminar facilitator's enthusiasm perfectly mirrors the threat Dennis fears
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold-open button. The timing of 'Who could possibly be happy right now?' as a rhetorical question immediately answered by a genuinely happy person singing about men's time being up is a structurally clean and funny juxtaposition. The irony is layered — the very thing Dennis fears arrives as a cheerful musical number. Strong construction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Nevada

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I gotta make some calls

jokes.text: Mac asks how many 'points' they need to get their name off the Shitty Bar List
jokes.setup: Kate begins the seminar by explaining why they're all there
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately gamifies it, asking about a point system — his brain can only process things competitively
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific absurdism. Mac reducing a harassment seminar to a points-based game is consistent with his jock-brained worldview. Sets up the Eagles callback efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: They got nothing on me past '92, tops

jokes.text: Frank shouts 'Statute of limitations!' as a non-sequitur question at the seminar
jokes.setup: Kate is trying to get through the introduction
jokes.punchline: Frank's non sequitur reveals he's not trying to learn — he's immediately doing legal triage on his own exposure
jokes.explanation: Economical and perfectly in character. The abruptness of 'Statute of limitations' — no preamble, just Frank's legal panic bursting through — is funnier than a complete sentence would be. It's both an absurd non-sequitur AND a logical response from Frank's perspective, which is the best kind of character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Some states like, uh, Nevada?

jokes.text: Frank: 'They got nothing on me past '92, tops.' — then walks out
jokes.setup: Frank learns the statute of limitations is 300 days from the last act
jokes.punchline: Frank confidently announces his legal position — which implies a lifetime of harassment with a specific cutoff date — and physically leaves, satisfied
jokes.explanation: 'Nothing on me past '92, tops' is quotable, dark, and perfectly Frank. The word 'tops' is doing enormous comedic work — it implies he's generously giving a pessimistic estimate of his own legal exposure. The physical act of simply leaving, satisfied, makes it a complete comedic beat. This is economy of craft at a high level.

dialogue.line: Oh! Here comes the boss man. Finally, a dude. Yeah, okay, cool. He's in charge.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Nevada, huh? Ah, it's getting warm in here. Got to make some calls. Shit.' — scrambles out
jokes.setup: Dennis has just invoked Nevada as a possible legal threat
jokes.punchline: Frank's instant panic response — 'calls to make,' implying he has people to warn or evidence to destroy — combined with 'shit' as a punctuation mark
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'shit' as the final word before exiting is a great button. The implication that he has a network of people to call about his Nevada exposure is rich with unstated dark comedy. 'Got to make some calls' says everything and nothing simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm gonna work really hard and get all the points

jokes.text: The gang immediately deferring to Alan (the male associate) over Kate (the female lead facilitator)
jokes.setup: Kate and Alan split the group for workshops
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately tries to defect to Alan — 'Finally, a dude. Yeah, he's in charge.' — perfectly illustrating the exact problem they're there to fix
jokes.explanation: The joke is irony as theme: the men at a sexual harassment seminar demonstrating the exact gender bias that necessitates sexual harassment seminars. Well-integrated into the episode's satirical framework.

dialogue.line: 'Go Birds' becoming a group rallying cry in the middle of harassment seminar

jokes.text: 'Well, that's how the Eagles won the Super Bowl.' / Dennis: 'I know that's how the Eagles won the Super Bowl, but this isn't the Eagles. This is a seminar.' / Mac and Charlie: 'Go Birds, though.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains there are no points, it's not football
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie harmoniously pivot to 'Go Birds, though' — a Philadelphia sports cheer offered as both a non-sequitur and an inarguable truth that ends the debate
jokes.explanation: The 'Go Birds' button is excellent. It escalates the running gag to its natural endpoint — not an argument, not a point, just an unconditional statement of Eagles loyalty that everyone (including Dennis) capitulates to. Dennis's reluctant 'All right, fine, go Birds. Yes' is the perfect straight-man collapse. The running gag has a satisfying arc.

dialogue.line: Role-play actor being criticized for mumbling his lines and not being believable rather than the harassment content

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Go Birds. Get your hand off my knee.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is briefly united over Eagles enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Dennis adds 'get your hand off my knee' as a seamless addition — implying someone (probably Mac) used the moment of sports camaraderie for uninvited physical contact
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. 'Go Birds. Get your hand off my knee.' is a two-clause sentence where the second clause is a complete non-sequitur that reveals an entire visual situation. It's also metatextually perfect — at a harassment seminar, Dennis is immediately dealing with unwanted physical contact. The delivery must be totally flat. One of the episode's best lines for efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. He mumbled his lines. I didn't believe a word out of his mouth.

jokes.text: Mac's description of his role: Dennis says 'He's our doorman' / 'No, he's just like our gay guy now'
jokes.setup: Alan asks Mac what he does at the bar; Mac says he's 'head of security'
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses him as a doorman; Charlie's reduction of Mac to 'our gay guy now' is both reductive and oddly affectionate, cutting through Mac's self-importance
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'our gay guy now' is funnier than Dennis's doorman correction because of its casual reductiveness. Mac is out as gay this season, and the gang treating it as a job title rather than an identity is characteristically oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: But it's not for her. It's about her

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: we haven't seen the girl's boobs. Can we see them?

jokes.text: Role-play actor mumbles 'boobs' line; Charlie's critique: 'He mumbled his lines. I didn't believe a word out of his mouth.'
jokes.setup: Alan asks what the boss did wrong in the role-play scenario (saying 'boobs' about an intern)
jokes.punchline: Charlie critiques the acting performance rather than the content — his only issue is craft, not ethics
jokes.explanation: Charlie's answer is a perfect misdirect — the audience expects someone to either 'get it' or miss it in a predictable way. Charlie goes sideways entirely and critiques the performance, which is funnier and more specific. Classic Charlie obliqueness.

dialogue.line: head of security
doorman
gay guy

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: what?

jokes.text: Mac offers to take his shirt off for the scenario to intimidate people, explaining it would compensate for Alan's height
jokes.setup: Alan suggests Mac do a role-play scenario as a doorman
jokes.punchline: Mac's first instinct is to remove his shirt — framed as tactical intimidation, but transparently an excuse to show off — delivered with complete earnest logic
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac vanity comedy. The tactical framing ('they won't be intimidated next to you but if I took my shirt off...') is perfectly in character — Mac wraps every bit of vanity in a logic-based justification. 'That's him doing his gay guy thing' from Charlie as the button is a good callback to the earlier line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I am the head of security at Paddy's Pub.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's our doorman.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, he's just like our gay guy now.

jokes.text: Charlie's scenario planning: 'Yeah, but why? I just drank three beers on the way over. You don't show up at a bar sober. What a waste of money.'
jokes.setup: Alan tells Charlie (in the scenario) that he's just trying to get into the bar to get a drink
jokes.punchline: Charlie elaborates pre-gaming logic from his actual life that is both absurd and weirdly consistent with his character's poverty/alcoholism
jokes.explanation: Charlie breaking the scenario to share his actual bar-going philosophy is very funny. 'What a waste of money' as a sincere economic objection to arriving sober at a bar reveals Charlie's budget-conscious alcoholism. High character integration score — this only works from Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Should I take my shirt off for intimidation? It's my gay guy thing.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I'm here for revenge.' — his character motivation for the scenario
jokes.setup: Alan just wants Charlie to play someone trying to get into a bar
jokes.punchline: Charlie invents an entire motivation — revenge — that is completely irrelevant to the scenario but entirely consistent with how Charlie approaches situations in real life
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie energy. 'I'm here for revenge' as a bar patron's motivation is both completely wrong for the scenario and completely correct for Charlie as a person. The commitment to it — not as a joke, but as a sincere character note — makes it land harder. High economy score for three words doing enormous character work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Not once has he ever checked an ID.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'And how many drinks have I had at this point?' Alan: 'You are... you're not in the scenario.' Dennis: 'I've had five.'
jokes.setup: Alan is trying to run a simple role-play scenario
jokes.punchline: Dennis inserts himself into a scenario he's not in, establishes he's had five drinks, and when corrected, simply states the number anyway
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'I've had five' after being told he's not in the scenario is a good beat — he's not arguing, just establishing facts that may become relevant. The confidence is very Dennis. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mac body-slams Dee, launching her 'a foot off the ground' the moment the scenario begins
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are doing a simple doorman/customer role-play. Dee approaches saying 'Excuse me, sir, have you...'
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately body-slams her without warning or justification, launching her into the air
jokes.explanation: One of the best physical gags in the episode. The abruptness — no escalation, no warning, Dee barely gets her first word out — is what makes it. The setup is mundane role-play; the punchline is immediate physical violence. 'That was amazing' and 'You got me like a foot off the ground' as the gang's reaction (treating assault as impressive athleticism) adds a second laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That was amazing! You got me, like, a foot off the ground!

jokes.text: Mac: 'She came at me and it was sort of my instinct.' Dee: 'That was great, right?' / 'You got me, like, a foot off the ground.' / 'Like Thumbelina. That's what I was going for!'
jokes.setup: Mac has just physically assaulted Dee in a role-play
jokes.punchline: Both Mac AND Dee are pleased with the result — Mac for the execution, Dee for the height achieved — treating a physical assault as a collaborative athletic achievement
jokes.explanation: The twist that Dee is not upset but proud ('That was great, right?') and both she and Mac have apparently done this before ('He's never gotten me that high before') recontextualizes the assault as a recurring bit between them. 'Thumbelina' as the shared reference point is an odd and funny specific choice.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And how many drinks have I had at this point? I've had five.

jokes.text: Dee stalls on answering whether Mac assaulted her, saying 'Now that I've gotten a little distance from the event...' while threatening to press charges
jokes.setup: Alan says Dee could press charges; Mac frantically asks Dee to tell Alan he didn't assault her
jokes.punchline: Dee deliberately milks the moment and gives an non-committal answer to maximize Mac's panic — weaponizing the scenario for personal leverage
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee move — exploiting any situation for personal gain/revenge. 'Now that I've gotten a little distance from the event' is a funny bureaucratic phrase applied to something that happened 60 seconds ago. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm like Thumbelina!

jokes.text: Mac starts sweating and says 'I feel like they crank up the heat' — the climate as a running anxiety metaphor
jokes.setup: Mac is now potentially facing assault charges; he starts physically sweating
jokes.punchline: He attributes his anxiety-sweat to the thermostat, echoing Frank and the earlier 'climate' joke
jokes.explanation: The 'climate' running gag — where every character uses temperature/climate as a euphemism for the cultural moment closing in on them — is a consistent throughline. Mac's version is functional but not the sharpest execution of it.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's the highest I've ever gotten.

jokes.text: Kate: 'The term sexual harassment wasn't coined until 1975 by a woman named Carmita Wood.' — Dee immediately repeating back 'Carmita Wood. Oh. I'm sorry. You really know your history.'
jokes.setup: Kate shares a historical fact about the term's origin
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately becomes an obsequious superfan of Kate's knowledge, performing feminist allyship for social credit
jokes.explanation: Dee's performative ally act is a good character beat — she's a terrible person who is opportunistically adopting feminist rhetoric because she thinks it benefits her. The 'Oh, I'm sorry' as a performative apology for no particular reason is a sharp specific detail.

jokes.text: Kate: 'Well, it's not very nice, but it's not sexual harassment.' Dennis: 'Nice try, you dumb bitch.'
jokes.setup: Dee's attempt to get Dennis in trouble via the seminar has failed
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately calls Dee a 'dumb bitch' — at the harassment seminar — the moment Dee's gambit fails
jokes.explanation: Perfect timing and economy. The instant pivot from Kate's ruling to Dennis's insult, delivered within the seminar context, is structurally excellent. It illustrates in real time exactly what a hostile work environment looks like. The irony is complete and sharp. 'Nice try, you dumb bitch' is delivered flatly as a matter-of-fact response, not as anger, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: if constantly calling a female coworker a bird is harassment

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Nice try, you dumb bitch

jokes.text: Dennis corrects Kate on federal harassment law: 'Federal law really only recognizes two types: quid pro quo and hostile work environment.'
jokes.setup: Dennis positions himself as a helpful, knowledgeable participant at the seminar
jokes.punchline: He just called Dee a 'dumb bitch' ten seconds ago; his pivot to legal pedantry is jarring and characteristically Dennis — doing predatory research to protect himself
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition — Dennis is simultaneously hostile work environment personified AND a legal expert on hostile work environment law. The fact that he's clearly done his research to protect himself reads as a dark character detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Quid pro quo, hostile work environment

jokes.text: Kate compliments Dennis; Dee: 'No, no, don't do that. This man is a monster. Believe you, me.'
jokes.setup: Kate praises Dennis for his legal knowledge
jokes.punchline: Dee's urgent warning 'this man is a monster' — delivered with the desperation of someone who has firsthand knowledge and no one will believe her
jokes.explanation: 'Believe you, me' is a funny archaism that fits Dee's desperation perfectly. The moment captures the genuine frustration of someone warning others about a dangerous person who appears charming. The show uses Dee as an accidental truth-teller here.

dialogue.line: Sir, that robe is inappropriate.

jokes.text: Frank returns in a bathrobe, on the phone: 'I bought her a Camaro... You know I don't go Chinese. Korean? Oh, put her on the list. I really did a number on her.'
jokes.setup: Frank left to 'make calls' about his Nevada exposure; he returns in a robe conducting damage control
jokes.punchline: His phone call reveals an ongoing, real-time cover-up — the Camaro as a payoff, the ethnic specificity of his preferences, and 'I really did a number on her' said without a trace of shame
jokes.explanation: The robe escalates the visual comedy from Frank's earlier sweat. His phone call is a cascade of incriminating details delivered as mundane logistics — 'I really did a number on her' said as a neutral assessment is the dark heart of Frank's character. The specificity of 'you know I don't go Chinese' as a preference for cover-up routes is a deeply weird and funny detail.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm buying him a Camaro, alright? No, no, I'm not going Chinese, but I'm considering Korean.

jokes.text: Kate: 'Sir, that robe is inappropriate.' Frank: 'Hon, I'm on the phone, you see?'
jokes.setup: Frank has shown up to the seminar in a bathrobe
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses Kate's legitimate concern with the condescending 'Hon, I'm on the phone, you see?' — not denying the robe's inappropriateness, just establishing phone call priority
jokes.explanation: 'Hon' as a condescending dismissal to the professional running the seminar is perfect Frank — unconsciously demonstrating the exact problem being addressed. The logic of phone call > propriety is very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank in a bathrobe making phone calls about finding women through abortion records

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh, I wish I was dead. These vultures are picking my carcass clean.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has pulled Frank outside to debrief; Frank has fully melted down
jokes.punchline: Frank's self-pity is completely inverted — he's the perpetrator describing accountability as predation on himself
jokes.explanation: The 'vultures picking my carcass' metaphor applied to being held accountable for harassment is a good dark comedy beat. Frank as the perpetrator-as-victim is a sharp satirical choice, delivered with his characteristic dramatic self-pity.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I wish I was dead. These vultures are picking my carcass clean

jokes.text: Mac's twitchy, sweaty re-entry into the hallway. 'Whoa, whoa, whoa. Which one of you just grabbed my ass?'
jokes.setup: Mac rejoins Dennis and Frank in the hallway, clearly rattled from the seminar
jokes.punchline: Mac is immediately groped — adding him to the list of harassment victims, at the harassment seminar, while they're all sweating about being harassers
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reversal — the harassers getting harassed at the harassment seminar. The abruptness of 'which one of you just grabbed my ass?' mid-conversation is well-timed. Dennis's response ('That is a problem for us') treating it as a tactical concern rather than a human complaint is good character work.

dialogue.line: Someone grabbing Mac's ass and him being confused about who did it, showing their powers are growing

jokes.text: Mac appears sweaty and disheveled from the other seminar room: 'I'm gonna be honest. The first half has not gone well.'
jokes.setup: Dennis told Mac to do absolutely nothing in the other room; Mac returns looking destroyed
jokes.punchline: Mac's catastrophically casual understatement — 'the first half has not gone well' — implies total disaster while sounding like a halftime sports assessment
jokes.explanation: The understated sports-halftime framing for what is clearly a catastrophe is very funny. Mac's physical state doing visual work while his words are breezy is good comedy construction.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Which one of you grabbed my ass?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Their powers are growing. Okay? We've got to start taking this more seriously.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been groped in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames the harassment seminar facilitators as a growing supernatural threat with 'powers' — treating a cultural accountability movement like a horror movie villain
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Dennis lines of the episode. 'Their powers are growing' applied to a #MeToo reckoning is a perfect encapsulation of Dennis's paranoid, self-centered worldview — he genuinely experiences accountability as a supernatural threat. Good economy, strong character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: flirting and groping

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: groping and dick pics

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie back in the seminar, asked what the two types of harassment are: 'Flirting and groping.' / 'Groping and dick pics. I know that sending dick pics is one of them.'
jokes.setup: Kate asks the group to recall the two types of harassment from earlier in the seminar (quid pro quo, hostile work environment)
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's answers reveal they absorbed absolutely nothing — their categories ('flirting and groping,' 'dick pics') are based entirely on news cycle awareness, not actual learning
jokes.explanation: Charlie and Mac's confident wrong answers are a good paired joke. 'I know that sending dick pics is one of them' as a statement of partial certainty while getting the category completely wrong is funny — Charlie has absorbed the cultural discourse but none of the legal framework. 'You're kidding. Christ.' from Dennis is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 'I like your tactic here. Get them all horny with your titties. That's when they make their mistakes.'

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I got to shoot some texts.' — responding to learning dick pics are not one of the legal categories
jokes.setup: Kate corrects that the actual types are quid pro quo and hostile work environment
jokes.punchline: Dennis's immediate response is to send texts — implying he was planning to send something that might constitute harassment and needs to reclassify or recall it
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark joke. 'I got to shoot some texts' is sufficiently vague to be funny without being explicit — the audience fills in what Dennis needs to communicate and to whom. Perfect Dennis characterization: immediate tactical response to new legal information.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Your tits are fine

jokes.text: Frank stares at Kate's chest throughout; Dennis interrupts: 'Please stop interrupting me.' Frank: 'Shit, I just looked at her tits.' / Dennis: 'Don't tell her that.' Frank: 'A passing glance is not sexual harassment.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been struggling to control himself throughout the seminar
jokes.punchline: Frank announces he looked at Kate's breasts as if reporting a minor incident; Dennis's PR response ('don't tell her'); Frank's self-citation of the law he just learned as immediate personal defense
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke that escalates nicely: Frank's confession, Dennis's crisis management, Frank's legal self-defense. Frank immediately applying newly-learned legal knowledge to his own behavior ('A passing glance is not sexual harassment') is both funny and character-perfect. He's learning from the seminar, just not in the intended direction.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What? I'm not allowed to like things anymore?

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh. I like your tactic here. Get them all horny with your titties. That's when they make their mistakes.' — said to Kate, thinking he's being helpful
jokes.setup: Kate has just said a passing glance is not harassment; Frank interprets this as tactical information
jokes.punchline: Frank reverse-engineers a conspiracy theory where Kate is using her appearance as an entrapment tactic, and congratulates her for it
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — he takes something normal and constructs an elaborate predatory interpretation that reveals more about his worldview than anything else. The 'I like your tactic' congratulation is patronizing and conspiratorial simultaneously. Kate's response ('that's victim blaming') and Dee's correction ('No, I'm blaming Frank. He's been staring at your boobs this whole time. Still doing it.') is a good three-beat payoff.

dialogue.line: The Waitress hypothetical scenario that exactly matches Charlie's actual stalking behavior

jokes.text: Dee: 'No, I'm blaming Frank. He's been staring at your boobs this whole time. Still doing it.' Frank: 'What? I'm not allowed to like things anymore?'
jokes.setup: Kate says Frank's attitude is victim-blaming
jokes.punchline: Frank's existential complaint — 'I'm not allowed to LIKE things anymore?' — reframes ogling as aesthetic appreciation being criminalized
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not allowed to like things anymore?' is an excellent line. The indignation, the framing of harassment as an expression of appreciation being suppressed, the genuine bewilderment — it's one of the more quotable Frank lines in the episode. High economy: five words do the work of a paragraph.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I-I think The Waitress is. Y-You know, 'cause, for-she doesn't realize that, like, true love is in front of her stupid face.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Well, they're not that great. Make her feel good.'
jokes.setup: Frank's 'it's a compliment' defense is challenged ('How is that a compliment?')
jokes.punchline: Frank issues a backhanded compliment — 'they're not that great' — while claiming he's being generous by saying anything at all
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank economy. He constructs an entire logic where staring at breasts that are 'not that great' and announcing this constitutes an act of generosity toward the recipient. The delivery must be sincere. Dark, character-specific, and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie

jokes.explanation: Excellent beat. Dennis's attempt to be the responsible adult in the room results in him doing the exact thing he's trying to prevent, with slightly better PR. 'Your tits are fine' as the reassurance aimed at the harassment seminar facilitator is structurally perfect irony.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I banged the Waitress when she needed a baby and was in women's shelter, plus everyone else banged her too

jokes.text: Kate's hypothetical scenario is transparently about Charlie's real-life stalking of The Waitress
jokes.setup: Kate describes a 'hypothetical scenario' about a customer who follows a coffee shop waitress home, digs through her trash, and calls repeatedly
jokes.punchline: The scenario is obviously Charlie's actual behavior with The Waitress, and the audience knows this — 'hypothetical' is doing all the work
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's more sophisticated jokes. Kate's supposedly neutral 'hypothetical' is a perfect recreation of Charlie's documented behavior with The Waitress, a character we know from the series. For regular viewers this is an enormously funny direct confrontation; it also works for new viewers as absurdist comedy of a character not recognizing their own behavior when described clinically. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I hate Seth. That guy's a creep.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I think The Waitress is [at fault]. You know, 'cause she doesn't realize that true love is in front of her stupid face.'
jokes.setup: Kate asks who is legally at fault in the stalking scenario
jokes.punchline: Charlie assigns fault to the victim for not recognizing his obsession as love, while also accidentally confirming this is about him ('The Waitress' — using her name)
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Charlie is entirely incapable of recognizing his own stalking as stalking — and furthermore believes The Waitress is culpable for not appreciating it — is both deeply character-specific and genuinely dark. Using 'The Waitress' by name outs the whole thing. The 'true love is in front of her stupid face' phrasing is both romantic and aggressive simultaneously, which is perfect Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, that makes sense. I always hated Seth. He's a real creep.

jokes.text: Mac's escalating details about the waitress scenario: '15 years later, when she needed a baby, really bad, and she'd been in and out of a women's shelter, he banged her.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to provide context that exonerates Charlie's character in the hypothetical
jokes.punchline: His context — the women's shelter, the desperate need for a baby, and the eventual sex — makes the situation dramatically worse while Mac presents it as exculpatory evidence
jokes.explanation: Dark escalation comedy. Mac's 'context' is a series of details that make Charlie look worse with every clause. 'In and out of a women's shelter' as a mitigating detail is especially dark. The gap between Mac's intent (defense) and the effect (indictment) is perfectly executed.

jokes.explanation: 'It wasn't very good, though' as an addendum to confirming sexual contact is a great timing beat. Mac's complaint about quality in this context — at a harassment seminar, recounting an encounter with someone he's currently discussing as a harassment victim — is perfectly oblivious.

jokes.punchline: Kate's answer (the boss) triggers Charlie to immediately identify the boss by name ('Seth') — blowing the entire hypothetical fiction
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Well, that makes sense. I always hated Seth.' perfectly demolishes the pretense that any of this was hypothetical. Charlie's total lack of awareness that he's just confirmed this is real — and that he has opinions about Seth — is classic Charlie obliviousness. The joke also rewards long-time viewers who know The Waitress's world. Perfect character integration and structure.

Alan's 'Well, now, actually, that is true' — which validates the molestation but not the conclusion — is funny because Alan seems to be processing multiple things at once and the acknowledgment comes out wrong.

'He got you big time' and 'you wrote a whole play about it' as receipts in an argument about whether someone was molested is blackly funny. The show uses its own lore (Charlie's one-man show about his childhood) as evidence.

jokes.explanation: The Thumbelina callback lands well because it recontextualizes the earlier physical comedy — Charlie's 'petite frame' argument now connects to him being literally launched by Mac earlier. 'It's a Thumbelina frame' is an unexpected and funny self-description that earns its callback. The logic that Dee's larger size constituted coercion is dark and absurd in equal measure.

jokes.punchline: Dee's reconstruction of her commands — which describe coercive behavior while being framed as evidence of normalcy — is so vivid and specific that Dennis recognizes it. His 'that's ringing a bell' implies he has heard/witnessed similar accounts.
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy at its best. Dee's verbatim reconstruction of her commands reads as an inadvertent confession — she's presenting evidence of coercion while arguing for consent. Dennis's 'that's ringing a bell' is a double-edged button: it confirms the account AND implies this is a recognized pattern, making Dee's situation worse.

jokes.setup: Dee invokes the 'women can't harass men' defense and appeals to Kate for sisterly solidarity
jokes.punchline: Kate: 'Actually, a woman can sexually harass and even rape a man.' — the perfect institutional deflation of Dee's appeal to gender solidarity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest structural jokes. Dee attempts a feminist solidarity play ('Back me up, girlfriend') to escape accountability; Kate's flat, authoritative correction turns the allyship appeal against Dee. The 'girlfriend' appeal being denied by the authority she's trying to co-opt is well-structured irony.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: 100% of men are capable of being sexual harassers. And 100% of women are capable of being sexually harassed.

jokes.text: Kate: 'Is that what happened here?' / Mac: 'Actually, maybe.'
jokes.setup: Kate has just confirmed women can rape men; she asks if that's what happened with Charlie and Dee
jokes.punchline: Mac's 'Actually, maybe' — a devastating understatement that opens the possibility that Charlie was raped, delivered as a mild conversational hedge
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. 'Actually, maybe' is a two-word sentence that opens an enormous and very dark comedic door while maintaining absolute deadpan. Mac's matter-of-fact delivery of a potentially catastrophic revelation for Dee is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's really only one thing that determines whether a person will be accused of sexual harassment, and that is... ugliness.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'No, no, no. You don't just throw around the R word, Kate. It's hot, right? Yello?'
jokes.setup: Kate and Mac have opened the possibility of Charlie being raped by Dee
jokes.punchline: Dennis tries to shut down the conversation about rape by simultaneously dismissing it, checking if the room is hot, and answering his phone — prioritizing temperature complaints and phone calls over a rape allegation
jokes.explanation: The 'Yello?' — answering a phone mid-sentence about a rape allegation — is a perfect Dennis moment. His crisis management strategy is to change the subject to temperature and take a call. The climate callback ('It's hot, right?') is woven in naturally.

jokes.punchline: Frank's matter-of-fact suggestion to locate someone through abortion records — a deeply invasive, possibly criminal suggestion delivered as routine problem-solving
jokes.explanation: One of Frank's darker background moments. The specificity of 'abortion records' as a tracking method implies Frank has a network and a history that is larger and darker than anything being discussed in the seminar. Delivered as a mundane logistics solution, which is the right comedic register. High character integration — this is uniquely Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis

jokes.explanation: Weaker moment in the episode. The crude insults here feel more exhausted than sharp — 'sucking a fat dick' as a performance critique doesn't have the specificity or character integration that the show's better dark jokes do. Dennis's 'you've sucked a dick through this process' is marginally funnier for its bureaucratic framing but it's still the episode's crudest and least crafted moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: A construction worker can catcall women all day long... nobody gives a shit, but a rich guy... A rich guy's fun to take down.

jokes.explanation: The cascading nature of Frank's phone disasters — each call revealing a new incident — is well-escalated. 'My dong fell out' as a reporting-to-crisis-management call is a funny specific euphemism for what is clearly a Harvey Weinstein-style incident, delivered with the gravity of a plumbing problem.

jokes.explanation: 'On your bikes' as a dismissal of the professional facilitators by the most dangerous person in the room is a good line. The irony is well-established — Dennis is the monster, taking over the monster-awareness seminar. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis's lecture: '100% of men are capable of being sexual harassers. And 100% of women are capable of being sexually harassed.' — followed immediately by walking back every implication
jokes.setup: Dennis has taken over the seminar and begins with an apparently reasonable statistical framework
jokes.punchline: He immediately dismantles his own premise through a cascade of 'of course not, no, absolutely not, but...' — the structure of someone who sounds reasonable but has nothing to say
jokes.explanation: Dennis's stream-of-consciousness walk-back ('of course not, no, absolutely not, no, yes... no') as a lecture introduction is sharp parody of corporate non-speak. The escalating hedges signaling that he has no actual point to make while performing expertise is a good Dennis character note.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis

jokes.text: Dennis: 'There's really only one thing that determines whether a person will be accused of sexual harassment... ugliness.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been building to his grand theory of harassment throughout his lecture
jokes.punchline: 'Ugliness' — the reduction of an entire social justice movement to aesthetics
jokes.explanation: The best single punchline in the episode and one of the sharper Dennis moments in the series. The long setup — the hedging, the statistics, the apparent reasonableness — lands on the most reductive, narcissistic, and weirdly insightful-about-Dennis possible conclusion. 'Ugliness' as the grand unified theory of harassment is both a sharp satire of a particular kind of male rationalization AND a perfect expression of Dennis's character. High scores across the board — this is the episode's anchor joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm neither [ugly nor sloppy]

jokes.text: Dennis presents a graph of ugliness vs. time and uses illustrated examples of an attractive vs. ugly man saying 'I like your dress'
jokes.setup: Dennis has established that ugliness determines harassment accusations
jokes.punchline: He literally has prepared graphs and illustrated examples — the preparation and presentation equipment reveals this is a belief system Dennis has developed and documented
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Dennis having prepared presentation materials — graphs, illustrated examples — for his ugliness theory is excellent. It implies he has thought about this extensively, rehearsed it, and considers himself a credentialed lecturer on the topic. 'Suddenly you're very uncomfortable. We're all uncomfortable just looking at him now. Because he's gross, he's ugly, he's a little bit of a monster.' — Dennis presenting himself as the attractive counterexample is the implicit punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Now is it this man's fault that he looks this way? No... but the point is, know your place, monster man. Your time's up.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has established that ugly men are inherently dangerous and can't help it
jokes.punchline: His conclusion — 'know your place, monster man. Your time's up' — is both compassionate (not your fault) and utterly contemptuous (you're a monster, go away)
jokes.explanation: 'Know your place, monster man' is a genuinely funny phrase — oddly compassionate in delivery while being completely dehumanizing in content. 'Your time's up' as the episode title callback adds a layer. Dennis's thesis is a parody of a certain kind of looks-obsessed rationalization, delivered with complete conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis

jokes.text: Dennis: 'If you're not sure [if you're ugly], probably best to assume that you are. Everyone in this room is. I did a scan.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is advising on how to assess one's own attractiveness
jokes.punchline: 'I did a scan' — Dennis has visually assessed every person in the room for attractiveness and reached a verdict, presented as due diligence
jokes.explanation: 'I did a scan' is possibly the most quotable line in the episode and among the best Dennis lines in recent seasons. The specificity and casualness of it — as if scanning a room for ugliness is a routine administrative task — is perfect character comedy. It reveals an entire system of behavior in three words. High scores across all dimensions: originality for the concept, economy for the execution, character integration because only Dennis would say and mean this.

jokes.explanation: The 'rich guy's fun to take down' argument has genuine satirical bite — it's an accurate observation about how public accountability works, filtered through Dennis's completely self-interested lens. The inversion of the expected wealth-as-protection argument is structurally good comedy.

jokes.explanation: 'Not willingly' is a great dark beat — it implies a history of Mac physically imposing affection on Dennis. This inverts Mac's victimization from earlier (the groping) and reveals Dennis also has a complaint. The 'it doesn't matter how much you work out' about Mac's physical obsession is a sharp specific cut. High character integration for both characters.

'Rifling through somebody's garbage' in the context of a harassment lecture is both a character-specific attack and a genuinely accurate description of Charlie's behavior.

jokes.explanation: Dennis getting genuinely sidetracked by his curiosity about whether Dee's hair is a wig — mid-lecture, mid-insult — is very funny. The pivot from 'your time's up' authority to genuine hair-related investigation before snapping back to 'doesn't matter. Your time's up' is a great rhythm. The 'lanky' callback to the bird running gag is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Mac: 'What year was that photo taken?' Dennis: 'No, no, no. Not taking questions right now, Mac.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is presenting a photo of himself as evidence of his physical excellence
jokes.punchline: Mac's question implies the photo is old — Dennis is using an outdated image — and Dennis's immediate refusal to take questions on that specific point
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and timing. Mac's one-sentence question demolishes Dennis's entire self-presentation without elaboration, and Dennis's PR-trained response ('not taking questions right now, Mac') acknowledges the problem while refusing to address it. The implication that this is a years-old photo he's presenting as current is very funny. High quotability — this is exactly the kind of exchange that gets clipped.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Would a woman really text that? ... Their phones did.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if women would really text consent confirmations
jokes.punchline: 'Their phones did' — the implication that Dennis sent the texts from their phones, or controlled the phones, making the 'consent documentation' manufactured evidence
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode by a significant margin. 'Their phones did' is two words that reveal an entire horrifying system — Dennis has been manufacturing consent documentation by using his partners' phones to send texts they did not send. The setup ('would a woman really text that?') appears to be Dennis genuinely questioning his own evidence, which makes the punchline both a confession AND a boast. Perfect economy (literally two words), maximum revelation, maximum character integration. This is the Dennis Reynolds character distilled to its most chilling essence. Comparable to 'their phones did' being one of the most economically perfect dark jokes the show has ever written.

jokes.text: Dennis reveals he created the Shitty Bar List himself, hired Kate and Alan, and fabricated the entire seminar to protect himself
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been premised on an external actor (an Internet warrior) putting Paddy's on the list
jokes.punchline: Dennis created the list, the seminar, and hired the facilitators himself — the entire elaborate trap is Dennis protecting himself while making it look like external accountability
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural reveal and one of its strongest comedy beats. The twist that Dennis engineered the entire situation — the list, the seminar, the facilitators — reframes every previous moment in the episode as Dennis managing a crisis of his own making while pointing blame elsewhere. 'Oh, yeah? Prove it.' as his button is perfect Dennis: immediate pivot to legal defense after a full confession. High structure and character integration scores.

jokes.text: Kate: 'You're a monster.' Dennis: 'Oh, yeah? Prove it.'
jokes.setup: Kate is horrified by the revelation that Dennis engineered the entire seminar
jokes.punchline: Dennis's instant 'prove it' — the reflexive legal defense of someone who has been anticipating this accusation and prepared accordingly
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the episode's big reveal. 'Oh yeah? Prove it.' immediately after confessing to creating the entire thing is Dennis in peak form — he has his documentation, he has his system, and he's immediately back on legal footing after the most damning admission of the episode. Maximum economy (four words), perfect character voice. One of the most quotable lines of the episode.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie applaud Dennis's reveal. Charlie: 'I didn't follow most of it, but so cool, man.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just revealed an elaborate self-protective conspiracy
jokes.punchline: Charlie's honest admission that he didn't understand the scheme but is enthusiastically impressed anyway
jokes.explanation: Good Charlie beat. 'I didn't follow most of it, but so cool, man' is perfectly in character — Charlie's enthusiasm is entirely uncoupled from comprehension. It also functions as a soft wink to any audience members who may have lost the thread.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Yeah, but it's true. Women are out to get us.' Dennis: 'Well, no. Men are monsters. We're constantly harassing them. I'm just saying we need to be more careful so we don't get accused. And we should probably stop harassing them.' Mac: 'Well, one step at a time.'
jokes.setup: The gang is debriefing after the seminar
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers the most minimal possible ethical improvement ('stop harassing them') as a step too far; Mac's 'one step at a time' treats it as an unreasonable demand
jokes.explanation: Very good closing beat. 'We should probably stop harassing them' treated as a radical suggestion — and Dennis himself only committing to 'one step at a time' — is the perfect dark punchline on the episode's theme. The gang has learned literally nothing, which is always the correct ending.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We don't want the whole system to collapse, you know what I mean? Ease into it.'
jokes.setup: The gang is slowly committing to 'stopping harassment'
jokes.punchline: Mac's concern that ceasing harassment could collapse 'the whole system' — treating harassment as a load-bearing structure of society
jokes.explanation: 'We don't want the whole system to collapse' is a brilliantly stupid framing. Mac treating systemic harassment as an infrastructure problem — requiring a phased withdrawal to prevent societal collapse — is a great satirical button. 'Ease into it' as the gang's unanimous conclusion on stopping harassment is the ideal episode-closing beat.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Very good. That's great. And for a woman, a good joke.'
jokes.setup: Kate has just made the MeToo pun
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'and for a woman, a good joke' — a condescending gender caveat on a compliment, at the conclusion of a harassment seminar
jokes.explanation: Perfect coda on the episode's theme. After an entire seminar on harassment, Dennis's first instinct upon hearing a good joke from a woman is to add a gendered qualifier to the compliment. This confirms — beautifully and efficiently — that nothing has changed. 'And for a woman, a good joke' is highly quotable and character-essential.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Hey, you guys think that Alan guy's got a big dick?' / 'Oh yeah.' / 'Huge.' / 'I saw it in the bathroom. I sought it out.'
jokes.setup: The gang is wrapping up after the seminar
jokes.punchline: Mac asks about Alan's anatomy; everyone immediately agrees; Mac confirms he actively investigated by seeking it out in the bathroom — the final beat of Mac's sexuality arc in the episode
jokes.explanation: 'I sought it out' is a great closer. The escalation from question to confident assertion ('huge') to firsthand confirmation ('I saw it in the bathroom') to the admission of active intent ('I sought it out') is a perfectly structured three-step escalation that ends on the most revealing detail. The episode's last joke confirming Mac is openly gay (and immediately acting on it) while Charlie and Dennis are entirely unbothered is a good warm close to an otherwise dark episode.

tmdb_overview: Paddy's has been put on a list of bars that are sexually hostile to women, and the gang must attend a sexual harassment seminar to get off the list.
